title: The yoga Krishna taught the sun
hookLine: a chain that runs back to the sun, and the Gita admits it broke
carry: parampara: a teaching lost, then told again
tomorrow: truth, discipline or study: what's worth teaching at home?

lines: THIS IS HOW IT WAS ALWAYS MADE.
I TAUGHT THIS TO THE SUN.
cards: Some family recipes come with a claim attached: this is how it was made back home, always. The Bhagavad Gita has a stranger claim than that.
Krishna and Arjuna are in a chariot between two armies when Krishna says: what I'm telling you isn't new. I taught it long ago to Vivasvat, the sun. Two odd things in a row.
How could he have taught the sun? And if the teaching is that old, why does Arjuna need it told again?

teach.b: The chain comes at the start of the Gita's fourth chapter. Krishna taught this lasting yoga to Vivasvat. Vivasvat told it to Manu.
Manu told it to Ikshvaku, a king. Handed down that way, the royal sages knew it. The Sanskrit for that handing down is parampara: one after another.
Then the next line solves the second puzzle.
Over a long stretch of time, Krishna says, this yoga was lost here. The Gita doesn't hide the gap.
So he tells it again, today, to one person. Why him? Because, he says, you are my devotee and my friend.
Arjuna catches the first puzzle himself. Your birth was later, he says, and Vivasvat's was earlier. How am I to understand that you taught him at the start?
The Gita lets him ask it out loud. Krishna answers: many births have passed, for me and for you. I know them all; you don't.
This is why Hindus still learn the Gita, a mantra or a prayer from a teacher's mouth, not only from a page: the teaching lives in parampara, teacher to student.
So a lineage, in this chapter, has three parts: a chain of people, a gap where the teaching goes quiet, and someone who picks it up again by speaking to the friend in front of him.

how: Some Hindu teachers and students recite the names of their line of teachers before study, and some learn the Gita from a teacher who learned it the same way.

o: a royal family's list of rulers and heirs
a teaching handed from one person to the next
a set of rules copied out of an old book

games.q: the chain in the Gita. tap the pairs.
p: told it to Ikshvaku, a king

s: in the Gita, the teaching passes along unbroken from the sun to Arjuna
Krishna says it was lost over a long stretch of time, so he tells it again.
Arjuna questions Krishna's claim to have taught Vivasvat
he says Krishna's birth was later and asks how to understand it.

games.q: you're Arjuna. Krishna has just said he taught this yoga to the sun, long ago. what do you say?
o: but you were born after him. how?
then teach me what the sun knows.
then this must be a royal secret.
games.why: Arjuna asks exactly that: your birth was later, Vivasvat's earlier. Krishna answers that many births have passed for both of them, and he remembers his.

practice: If you know a prayer, a mantra or a few lines of the Gita that someone taught you, say them once, slowly, out loud. Picture the person who taught you, and the one who taught them.
If you don't pray, do the same with any words someone handed to you, a saying or a song. That's parampara, one link long.

wordCard.voice: A lineage: parampara, one after another. In the Gita, it can be lost, and told again.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one after another. In Gita 4.2 the yoga comes down this way, from teacher to teacher.

carryVoice: For the road: parampara, a teaching lost, then told again. In the Gita, it begins again when one friend tells another.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.1–4.3 (Krishna taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat, Vivasvat to Manu, Manu to Ikshvaku; handed down thus, the royal sages knew it; by a long lapse of time it was lost here; told again today to Arjuna, devotee and friend)
Bhagavad Gita 4.4–4.5 (Arjuna: your birth was later, Vivasvat's earlier; Krishna: many births have passed for me and for you; I know them all, you do not)
